title: Optimizing Recovery After an Ultramarathon (CTS, updated 2025-04-22)
population: Coach guidance for ultramarathoners, mainly after a 100-mile race
findings: Days 1 to 3: 'There is nothing to be gained by rushing through these early days.' The page says to try to get up and walk for at least a few minutes a few times per hour (circulation and stiffness) early on.
Week 1: no runs over 20 minutes. Weeks 2 and 3: recovery-paced runs only, kept under 1 hour.

Sleep 8 to 10 hours on a regular basis for at least two weeks; the month after a 100-miler is a good time for other activities (swimming, easy cycling, yoga, kayaking, paddle boarding); adequate energy intake is essential.
A well-prepared athlete 'maybe' returns to training after a few weeks; for athletes who were unprepared and made major mistakes, recovery could take several weeks or months.
Readiness: an athlete is ready when 'excited to train again and feels physically fresh and energetic'.
limitations: Convention from one coach, no data cited on the page fetched; no explicit distance-specific figures for 50 km or 100 km.
implications: Gives a concrete shape: week 1 at most 20 min runs, weeks 2 and 3 recovery pace only and under 60 min, which can serve as a convention source for the 100-mile ramp.
Supports a feel-based gate (motivation and freshness) that can delay but, because of the Hoffman data, should not on its own advance the schedule.

verification.notes: Re-fetched the page twice with WebFetch: author Jason Koop, 'April 22, 2025', the 20 minute week-1 limit, weeks 2-3 under 1 hour, sleep, walking, cross-training and readiness quotes all present. 'Do not cut calories' reworded to the page's 'adequate energy intake is essential'; 'paddling' corrected to kayaking and paddle boarding. Practice source (programme, coaching or clinical page): a published convention, not evidence; grade D.

interests: CTS sells coaching, training plans, camps and testing; the page's author is CTS's head ultrarunning coach, and the site promotes his book Training Essentials for Ultrarunning.

r1.note: The week-1 limit of 20 minutes, weeks 2 and 3 under 1 hour, 8 to 10 hours of sleep for two weeks, energy intake, other activities in the month after and the readiness line all located on the page fetched 2026-10-31 (published 2025-04-15, updated 2025-04-22).

r2.note: Author named on the page (Jason Koop, CTS head ultrarunning coach). Independent record: Outside Run's 2015 article (read 2026-10-31) describes him as director of coaching at Carmichael Training Systems; the CTS bio is the employer's page. Interests recorded: CTS sells coaching and Koop's book.

r3.note: The version read is the one updated 2025-04-22, the date in the record. No later corpus paper gives a return-to-run protocol (millet-2011, hoffman-2017 and garciavaliente-2026 describe damage and recovery time only).

r4.note: Weeks of reduced running agree in shape with Roche (skurka-2017) and Powell (irunfar-2016), independent coaches, and function data (millet-2011, hoffman-2017) show recovery by days 5 to 16. Roche and Powell differ on the week-1 dose (rest versus short jogs); the conservative reading is the shorter run.

r5.note: Population is coach guidance for ultramarathoners, mainly after a 100-mile race; the record states there are no figures for 50 km, and the H12 Param notes label the extension to other classes as a default. second pass: h12.step2RunMaxMin and h12.reducedDays apply this 100-mile advice to the later steps after a marathon or a 50K, and their notes name the 100-mile plans without calling that extension an extrapolation.

r6.note: Evidence level D, at the practice cap.

vetting.signedOff: two independent reading passes, S4 and S4b, 2026-10-31
